#3260. Goosehead (GSHD) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Restatement lifts revenue while Texas pricing pressure weighs on the quarter.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Goosehead Insurance, Inc. (GSHD -1.56%) reported preliminary third quarter results alongside a notification of a pending financial restatement concerning prior periods. Management indicated that the restatement, which involves the capitalization of certain agent commissions and the reclassification of franchise technology fees, is expected to result in an increase in reported operating income and total revenue for affected years. The company observed a healing personal lines insurance market with expanded carrier appetite and stabilized pricing, although these factors contributed to downward pressure on premium retention as the market softened. Strategic focus shifted toward penetrating the partnership ecosystem through enterprise sales and embedded franchise models while preparing for technological shifts in client interaction.

Operator: Good day, and thank you for standing by. Welcome to the Goosehead Insurance Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please be advised that today's conference is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to your speaker for today, Maddie Middleton. Please go ahead.

Maddie Middleton: Thank you, and good afternoon. Before we begin our formal remarks, I'd like to address the Form 8-K we filed today. As disclosed in that filing, our previously issued annual and quarterly financial statements for and as of the years and quarterly periods in 2023, 2024 and 2025 and our quarterly financial statements for the first half of 2026 should no longer be relied upon. Our review remains ongoing, so any estimated impacts we discuss today to reflect our preliminary and current expectations have not been reviewed or audited and may change as the review progresses. We will distinguish previously reported amounts from any updated amounts presented on the call where applicable.

I also need to remind everyone that part of our discussion today may include forward-looking statements, which are based on expectations, estimates and projections of management as of today. Forward-looking statements in our discussions are subject to various assumptions, risks and uncertainties and other important factors that are difficult to predict and which could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied in the forward-looking statements. These statements are not guarantees of future performance, and therefore, undue reliance should not be placed on them. We refer you all to our recent SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of risks, uncertainties and other important factors that could impact future operating results and financial condition of Goosehead.

We disclaim any intention or obligation to update or revise any forward-looking statements, except to the extent required by applicable law. I would also like to point out that during the call, we will discuss certain financial measures that are not prepared in accordance with GAAP. Management uses these non-GAAP financial measures in planning, monitoring and evaluating our performance. We consider these non-GAAP financial measures to be useful metrics for management and investors to facilitate operating performance comparisons period-to-period by including potential differences caused by variations in capital structure, tax position, depreciation, amortization and certain other items that we believe are not representative of our core business.

For more information regarding the use of non-GAAP financial measures, including reconciliations of these measures to the most recent comparable GAAP financial measures, we refer you to today's press release. In addition, this call is being webcast, and an archived version will be made available shortly after the call ends on the Investor Relations portion of the company's website at goosehead.com. I'd like to turn the call over now to our CEO, Mark Miller.

Mark Miller: Thanks, Maddie, and thank you all for joining us this afternoon. As I'm sure some of you have seen by now, we filed an 8-K regarding our previously issued financial statements. These adjustments have no impact on our cash flows or business operations, but they result in an increase in reported revenue and earnings in the affected periods. John Martin will walk through the specifics and their financial impact later in the call. We're proud of our third quarter performance, and that's where I'd like to focus our discussion today. Total revenue grew approximately 17% and core revenue grew 13% from the prior period.

These are strong results, and I believe they reflect something bigger than the performance of any single quarter. We've spent years building one of the largest organically grown personal lines insurance businesses in the country, and those investments have positioned us to capitalize on an increasingly attractive market opportunity. I want to spend a few minutes talking about why I believe that opportunity is so significant. The personal lines insurance product market has healed considerably. Carrier appetite has expanded, capacity has returned and pricing has stabilized across much of the market. The result is a healthier, more competitive environment with more options available to consumers than we've seen in years.

For Goosehead, this is exactly the type of environment where our model demonstrates its full value. We now have more than 2,800 agents nationwide, providing local expertise in their respective markets. Our robust product offering allows us to serve approximately 98% of homeowners across the country. When carriers are competing for business, our agents can do what they do best: evaluate clients' individual needs and find the right coverage with the right carrier at the right price. When we get that right, we've established a relationship built on trust that can last for years. Our opportunity isn't simply to sell more policies.

It's to build lasting relationships in a market where the value of an independent agent has never been more apparent. The improvement in the product market is happening against a challenging housing market. Home closing transactions are at a 30-year low. To some extent, this is a headwind on lead flow from our traditional referral partner marketing. However, every homeowner needs insurance, whether they purchased their home yesterday or 30 years ago. If you live somewhere or drive something, you need our product. Now operating across 11 states, our corporate team diversifies our geographic presence, develops new referral partner relationships and most importantly, provides a pipeline of talent for future franchise owners. We're also building around our strongest franchises.

Our franchisees continue to hire and become more productive. This quarter, we reached a record 2.6 producers per franchise and over $30,000 in average monthly gross compensation per franchise with some approaching $1 million per month. We're sharpening the profile of the franchise owners we recruit, targeting experienced business operators and investors with the capital and leadership to scale rapidly while continuing to develop franchise owners from our corporate agent base. The corporate franchise flywheel continues to gain momentum with more than 180 franchise producers working in agencies owned by former corporate agents. We're expanding through mortgage originators, servicers and strategic partners.

We've launched 12 embedded franchisees within businesses with established customer lead flow with new business production up 64% from the third quarter of last year for these agencies. In some cases, we have seeded these new partnerships with experienced Goosehead talent to enable them to scale rapidly. This has become a strategic pillar of the corporate sales team. Alongside these partnerships, enterprise sales expands our reach through institutional relationships, primarily outside the home-closing transaction. Together, these channels diversify lead flow, allow partners to offer insurance at scale and deliver the quality of clients our carriers expect. Over the past several years, we've invested heavily in service, both in our people and technology. Those investments are paying off.

Retention is steadily improving, and our existing clients are referring friends and family to Goosehead. Our human agents now answer calls in less than 30 seconds, over 70% of the time. And our client satisfaction score is consistently 4 out of 5, and we only expect that to improve. None of this happens without the infrastructure we've spent years building. We've equipped our agents with the most comprehensive product portfolio in the industry and powerful proprietary technology tools that enable them to drive industry-leading productivity. In the first half of this year, we put that technology in clients' hands through a true digital choice shopping experience. We've always believed the future of insurance is both digital and human.

Clients want convenience alongside the guidance of a trusted agent and our omnichannel platform gives them both. But technology alone doesn't create a successful insurance business. It takes carrier relationships, product breadth, knowledgeable agents and service that supports clients long after the sale. When you look at these opportunities together, the strength of Goosehead becomes clear. Over the last 20-plus years, we've built a world-class service organization, developed proprietary technology that sets us apart, attracted and developed exceptional talent and established deep trusted relationships with our carrier partners. Each of these capabilities is a competitive advantage on its own.

Together, they create a business that is extremely difficult to replicate, and we've done it with one primary focus in mind: the client. The client always has been and always will be the center of our universe. My confidence in Goosehead's teammates, strategy, purpose and future has never been stronger. Now I'd like to turn it over to Mark Jones, Jr., our President and Chief Operating Officer.

Mark Jones Jr.: Thanks, Mark. That very commitment to the client has shaped our business since the beginning and continues to guide the investments we're making for tomorrow. Advancements in technology are allowing us to adapt how we engage with clients at a rapid pace. Our service function is now reachable through channels that weren't available even a few years ago, places like our web portal, mobile app and AI voice assistant Lily. With no pressure from us to dictate how clients choose to interact, they are naturally selecting the option that works best for them.

More service work than ever is being completed entirely through digital channels, nearly 1/3 of the total workload, all within the safeguards we've put in place to protect clients and carriers alike. Our clients are telling us our technology, when pointed at the right specific actions, delivers just as high quality of service as our world-class team members with a client satisfaction score on digital channels of 4.1 out of 5. The impact of that technology is felt directly in our cost to serve. Our service cost per policy in force has consistently come down over the last year, all while service levels have improved.

What I find most interesting, however, is clients are still choosing to interact with a member of our service team even when their requests could be completed entirely through digital channels. Clients want human interaction because there's a very real human element to insurance. It's complicated, not intuitive and the cost of getting it wrong can be severe. Many clients interacting with us are in the middle of a stressful situation. They may be in the process of purchasing their first home and want to talk through all the specifics of the coverage for what is now likely their largest asset.

They may have just had a child turn 16 and need to add them to their auto coverage, all while dealing with the emotion of having a new driver in the house. They could be filing a claim after an event that's turned their life upside down. Our job is to be there for our clients wherever and however they need us, not force them through the most cost-effective path. That is how we build lasting trust. On the sales side, to be where our clients want to interact, we are designing our technology so that Goosehead's capabilities can power the insurance experience across a range of interfaces.

For example, if a client chooses to begin their shopping experience through their favorite AI assistant, Goosehead will be positioned to serve them there. We're in the process of building a Model Context Protocol, or MCP server, on top of our existing services and capabilities to enable those connections. We expect that to be live by the end of this year. We're also improving our Generative Engine Optimization, or GEO, to make it easier for AI models and agents to find and interact with us.

These enhancements will more easily allow AI agents working on a client's behalf to engage with Goosehead and shop across our unmatched carrier network in a way that provides the appropriate context for differences in coverage and avoids boiling down a complex process solely to price. We've stayed close to our carrier partners on this topic. In recent discussions, one thing remains clear: carriers are continuing to invest in the independent agent distribution channel. Today, agents place north of 70% of the $560 billion personal lines market with independent agents continuing to take share from captives. Today, our digital agent allows clients to go from quote to issue entirely within our digital flows.

However, while they can choose this path, the vast majority of clients still choose to complete the purchase after consulting one of our local agents. Our carriers are telling us their experience in new channels matches ours. While the market may change over time and that total distribution share may shift into new channels, a considerable portion of the total addressable market is likely to persist in agent-led channels for the foreseeable future. We are positioning our model to be channel agnostic. We will have the ability to support clients digitally as they shop through whichever channel they prefer, while giving them the confidence of a licensed agent to review coverage and confirm placement of the policy.

We have consistently invested ahead of changes in how clients shop for insurance, and we intend to keep building for wherever they choose to engage next. Turning to some specifics on the third quarter results. Our total producer count, inclusive of corporate, enterprise and franchise producers was 2,840, up 7% year-over-year. We sustained strong levels of new business production with new business commissions growing 21% year-over-year and new business royalty fees up 13% year-over-year. We anticipate delivering full year new business commission growth at its fastest pace since 2021 and full year new business royalty fee growth at an accelerated pace over the previous year.

Our strategic partnerships are driving real growth in new business, which can be seen in our enterprise sales team. Now with over 150 agents, this team's new business growth rate is greater than 50% for the third quarter, their eighth consecutive quarter of greater than 50% growth, and we anticipate that to accelerate in the fourth quarter. Our executed partnerships in total now represent over 5 million potential clients and provide a captive audience with a data advantage that allow us to grow new business production at rates that would have previously been more closely tied to head count growth.

As our Digital Agent technology continues to mature and new features and geographies are added, we anticipate further adoption of the end-to-end binding capability that is available within a choice model only at Goosehead. As the product market has normalized and pricing has fallen year-over-year, that provides us the opportunity to add more value to our clients by identifying those that may be overpaying for their existing coverage or who now have options for additional coverages and assist in placing them with an underwriter with a more competitive offering.

The result is a short-term headwind to renewal revenue, but a long-term improvement in client retention as clients feel the true value of the Goosehead model acting as a trusted advocate on their behalf. Looking into the coming years, our core strategic pillars are simple: continuously improve the client experience and look for opportunities to take part in those improved outcomes; invest in our technology to provide access to clients in whatever channel they choose, be it through a live agent, personal AI assistant, Goosehead website or mobile app; expand our human capital advantage through our distribution forces; and penetrate deeper into the partnership ecosystem to expand revenue growth opportunities.

We have an exceptional team and an incredible runway for continued growth. This dynamic environment is tilted in Goosehead's favor as our focus remains squarely on our clients. With that, I'll turn the call over to John Martin to give you an update on our current financials and provide outlook for the remainder of the year. John?

John Martin: Thanks, Mark, and good afternoon, everyone. Before turning to our third quarter performance, I'd like to provide some additional color around the 8-K we filed relating to prior period financial results. In connection with the standard and ongoing review of our annual filings, we received a comment letter from the staff of the SEC regarding certain disclosures in our 2025 10-K, including our accounting for cost to obtain contracts with customers. Our North Star has always been ensuring that our financials both accurately portray the economic reality of the business and are fully compliant with GAAP. Our historical approach to the recognition of agent compensation costs has been to expense them as incurred.

While we believe this treatment reflects the underlying fundamentals of our operations, we have determined this approach does not conform with FASB standards, which require a portion of these costs to be deferred over a determined useful life. As a result, we have concluded it is necessary to restate our previously issued financial statements and recognize a portion of our compensation expense over a longer period of time. In conjunction with this evaluation, we initiated a comprehensive review of our broader accounting policies. Through this process, we identified an additional adjustment around the presentation of certain franchise-related fees, which largely pertain to technology cost recovery.

These fees were historically presented as a G&A expense offset and should be reclassified as revenue. After careful consideration, the Audit Committee of the Board of Directors, together with management, have determined the resulting adjustments are material to certain previously issued financial statements. These include those related to the annual periods 2023, 2024 and 2025 and the interim periods Q1 and Q2 in 2026. Accordingly, we are working to finalize and file restatements for the affected periods as well as for our third quarter 10-Q as soon as practical. The restatement impact related to these 2 items is straightforward. First, the compensation cost piece.

There is less expense in-period and more placed on the balance sheet, which then amortizes over the expected benefit period. We preliminarily expect compensation expense to decrease and operating income to increase by approximately 0.5% to 5.5% of total employee compensation and benefits for each of the full year 2025 and the first half of 2026. Second, the reclassification of certain fees charged to franchises. The impact here is simply a one-for-one gross up of both total revenue and G&A expense by the same dollar amounts and in the same periods. We preliminarily expect the impact to be approximately $11 million to $16 million in 2025 and approximately $8 million to $13 million over the first 3 quarters of 2026.

As a final comment on this topic, I'd highlight 2 primary takeaways. First, there is no change at all to our core revenues, cash flows or the underlying economics of the business. And second, we expect the presentation impact in our restated financials to reflect increases in total revenues, operating income and adjusted EBITDA. And with that, let's turn to our performance highlights for the third quarter. Policies in force grew 14% year-over-year to $2.1 million and total written premiums grew 11% year-over-year to $1.3 billion. Total revenues grew 17% year-over-year to $110 million, reflecting the midpoint of the range provided in our press release. Core revenues grew 13% year-over-year to $95 million.

Similar to last quarter, we're pleased to see our growth driven by a combination of strong new business performance, improving retention and increases in contingent commissions. New business commissions grew 21% year-over-year to $9.1 million, and new business royalties grew 13% year-over-year to $9.4 million. Recruiting is stronger than ever with our aggregate producer base now up 7% year-over-year for a total of 2,840 producers. As we've grown the producer base, we've continued to diversify our footprint into untapped markets, and we now have more than 65% of corporate agents located outside of Texas. In the past year alone, this mix has increased nearly 20 percentage points.

We're encouraged to see our enterprise sales team contribute outsized growth as we continue to deepen our strategic partnerships. Enterprise sales grew head count 71% year-over-year and contributed 23% of total new business commissions and agency fees. On the franchise side, our agency owners are leaning heavily into growth with same-store sales up 29% year-over-year for our top 50 franchises, and up 17% year-over-year for the entire channel. Corporate agent-launched franchises are punching well above their weight class. These agencies represented 6% of total producers and contributed 15% of total new business production in the third quarter. It's great to see our thesis playing out here in real time.

Client retention remains significantly improved at 86% and represents one of our largest opportunities as we continue to execute against initiatives that improve the overall client experience. Ancillary revenues, largely comprised of contingent commissions, grew 106% year-over-year to $10.3 million. This quarter's results and our continued positive outlook on contingents are driven by favorably negotiated contracts with carriers, the volume and quality of new business written and minimal cat losses. We ended the quarter with $33 million of cash and cash equivalents and $322 million of total debt outstanding. As the restatement work remains ongoing, we intend to focus the balance of today's discussion, including Q&A, on key business drivers and operating trends, which we can speak to with confidence.

We'll provide a more fulsome discussion of expenses and profitability once the financial statements are finalized. Turning now to the balance of the year. We are reiterating our revenue and total written premium outlook for the full year 2026. We continue to expect total revenues to grow organically in the range of 12% to 19% year-over-year and total written premiums to grow organically in the range of 12% to 20% year-over-year. Finally, stepping back from the numbers, I continue to be incredibly encouraged by the breadth of progress we're seeing. We are expanding our producer base and geographic reach. Our franchise owners are growing and client retention has improved meaningfully. These are mutually reinforcing strengths.

Our distribution brings more customers into the business, while our service, technology and carrier relationships help us deliver more value to them over time. In a large and fragmented market where our share remains small, we believe that combination gives us a substantial runway for continued growth. Thank you to our teammates, franchise owners and partners for their effort that drives our progress. And thank you to everyone joining us today for your continued support of Goosehead. With that, I'd like to turn it back over to Mark Miller for closing comments.

Mark Miller: Thanks, John. Before we open up for questions, I want to say a few words as this is my final call as CEO of Goosehead Insurance as I'm retiring at the end of the year. It's been an extraordinary journey, and I'm incredibly grateful to our teammates, our agents, our carrier partners and our shareholders for everything they've done to make this so rewarding. As I transition out of this role, I'm incredibly proud of the strength of the company today and excited for the opportunities ahead. I believe Goosehead has never been stronger, more capable or better positioned to deliver sustained profitable growth than it is today.

Over the past several years, we've been very intentional about strengthening our leadership team, investing in our technology and infrastructure and building the capabilities we need to support the company's long-term growth. Mark Jones Jr. has played an important role in virtually everything we've done to prepare Goosehead for this next chapter. He's helped shape our strategy, strengthen our operations and build the foundation for the future. I have tremendous confidence in Mark and our leadership team and in the direction of the company. This is a natural transition for the business, and I believe it positions Goosehead extremely well for the years ahead.

I firmly believe Goosehead's best days are still in front of us with Mark at the helm. It's been an incredible privilege to serve as CEO. Thank you for your trust, your partnership and your support throughout this journey. With that, I'll open it up to questions. Operator?

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Our first question will be coming from the line of Tommy McJoynt of KBW.

Thomas Mcjoynt-Griffith: The first one here is around some of your remarks on building bridges for personal AI agents. I think you mentioned you guys are developing a Model Context Protocol to build that bridge. Is that going to entail Digital Agent 2.0 fully bindable quotes being available to be bound by personal AI agents? And along those lines, do you have to get your trusted carrier partners to opt in to that type of integration? Or generally, what is the feedback from your carrier partners around this?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. Thanks, Tommy. This is Mark. So we've spent a lot of time being very close to our underwriters on this topic, specifically on what's the right way for personal AI agents to interact with the distribution channel. And ultimately, we want to be available wherever clients are attempting to interact with.

And so if we can make our Digital Agent technology available to personal AI agents in a way that is safe, protects us from a cybersecurity perspective and provides the appropriate context, and so you can actually compare different types of coverages because not all policies are the same, that's how we can get lasting trust with our underwriters to allow us to be a trusted intermediary in a way that can prevent them from rapidly accumulating business that's not going to be profitable for them. But we'll see how that technology develops over time. There's still some open regulatory question marks surrounding that topic, but we want to be able to be wherever our clients want to interact.

Thomas Mcjoynt-Griffith: Okay. Got it. And then I think you said -- you gave some metrics around new business production at your embedded partners working with mortgage servicers and other types of entities that it grew, I think you said, over 64% year-over-year. What percentage of your total new business production does that channel now represent? And when I think about the growth there, is that in any way cannibalizing any of your other business that you would have had through a different channel previously?

Mark Jones Jr.: Great question, Tommy. So right now, the embedded franchise partners, which is -- this is an important distinction, those are partnerships in which that entity owns its own Goosehead franchise, those have grown really well over the last year. They don't make up a super material portion of franchise new business production, but it's becoming more impactful, and they're now some of our largest franchises. If you think about the entire partnership ecosystem, that would include everything from our enterprise sales team. And that's starting to become a reasonably material portion of the business and continuing to grow at a super rapid pace.

To your point on cannibalization, because we specifically focused on people like mortgage servicers as opposed to intentionally going after originators first, there's not really a cannibalization effect. And also remember, we're still at very low penetration into the home-closing total addressable market. So I don't believe we've cannibalized any of our existing lead flow. This is all incremental to what the current business is doing.

Operator: Our next question will come from the line of Brian Meredith of UBS.

Brian Meredith: A couple here. First, I'm just curious, if I look at your core revenue growth of 13%, it slowed from the second quarter. Anything kind of behind that? What's going on there?

John Martin: Brian, it's John. Just to call out a few items here. One, we're extremely proud of the 13% we were able to put out in the third quarter. I'd say there's a couple of areas I'd highlight here. One, a bit tougher comparisons in the third quarter than in the second quarter. Two, we're seeing a bit more pricing than we had previously anticipated in our core market specifically, and that's more of an external factor that we obviously don't control. But we feel good about how we're responding and what we actually need to do to execute and maintain control around the core controllables.

And so that includes growing our producer count, growing productivity, leaning more into the partnerships and fulfilling that through enterprise sales among other channels. And so we feel really good about the business, and let's say that.

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. And then if you look at the new business numbers, I think it was a pretty strong new business quarter. I mean corporate new business commissions up 21%. The franchise business grew 13% in terms of new business generation. Really where you're seeing the impact is pricing in the Texas book for the corporate side of the business. That's been probably a larger decline in pricing than what we would have expected even 3 months ago. But the rest of the business is generally performing very well, and we're still seeing progress in terms of client retention. It's just that the pricing impact in Texas specifically has been a lot bigger than what we probably initially anticipated.

Brian Meredith: Great. And I'm just curious, maybe give an update on the number of carriers, any new ones participating on your aggregator platform?

Mark Jones Jr.: In terms of the Digital Agent?

Brian Meredith: Digital Agent, yes, Digital Agent, sorry. Yes. And like new carriers on there, kind of the progress there on Digital Agent.

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. So we've made a lot of progress on Digital Agent, really hardening the technology to make sure it can scale to the size that we want it to scale at. We're obviously still incredibly proud to have what we believe, I think, is still the only choice shopping model where our clients can go quote to issue all the way through. And for us, the interesting learning is we're getting thousands of people at the top end of the funnel here. And the vast majority of them, somewhere throughout the process, want to kick out and talk to a human being because we largely lead with the homeowners. So that's a pretty complex process.

And we're going to continue to make UI, UX and educational information available in the Digital Agent to continue to increase the share that we believe can go all the way through the process. But what nobody else is really, I believe, able to replicate is that human capital infrastructure across the entire country where effectively almost anybody starting at the top end of the digital binding flow can kick out and talk to a digital agent who is largely inside their local area. So we're going to keep investing in that technology. I still believe that is the future of the organization.

But you're not going to get away from the need to have that human capital on the back end, and that's the piece that's really hard to replicate.

Brian Meredith: And is Digital Agent going to be able to work with like the Meta Muse?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. So that's part of the MCP process that we're working through is to be able to allow personal AI agents to engage with us in a safe way that minimizes risk to carriers and minimizes risk to clients, right? There's a whole host of questions that still need to be answered is, has the client officially requested that their agent go attempt this task? Or did they give it a loose parameter like manage my finances and this is something that they've decided this on managing a finance-type activity, or did it give express consent to go run a new insurance quote?

So there is a whole host of questions that still need to be answered on that topic, but we want to build the functionality to be able to engage in those channels in a way that provides our carriers with good access and allows our clients to choose how they interact.

Brian Meredith: Got you. And any change in carrier partners in the Digital Agent?

Operator: The next question is coming from the line of Randy Binner of Texas Capital Securities.

Randy Binner: I'd like to follow up on the first question and just maybe like higher level, in the third quarter or in this current quarter, it sounds like you're not seeing direct impact from AI agent activity in the market, but just kind of on a more simple level, I just want to kind of emphasize that. It sounds like most of your customers are still talking to the agents, but just in the market, are you seeing an impact from perhaps other carriers who are engaging with AI agents? Or is it too early in that process?

Mark Jones Jr.: No, it's still really early in that process. And we have talked to the majority of all of the major underwriters. So you could think of a pretty considerable portion of the independent agent distribution market share. We've had conversations at the most senior levels about how we think this is going to play out. And everybody's thoughts are generally the same. They're seeing an increase in bot activity. And I think this probably helps with the information-gathering of their direct businesses, but does not replace independent agent distribution. It's just a fundamentally different shopper. And I can give you one anecdotal example.

We've got our own team internally who -- we're constantly checking the capability sets of these tools just to make sure we understand what's currently available and how can we cater to those technologies. And you can send out 2 different bots with all of the same information. They can go run from the carrier direct-to-consumer websites, auto quotes, with the same information, pull back quotes from the same carrier and get 25% differences in price. So if you're an underwriter, that's got to be a pretty frightening proposition. I'm not sure exactly how that issue gets solved, but that's not an issue that you run into with an independent agent.

And then the other point I would make on this topic is the cost of getting that information wrong. So you've probably heard the phrase liability transfer with respect to this topic before. If you're using your own personal AI agent to go get you insurance policies, you're transferring all the risk of those policies being wrong to yourself.

So the cost of getting it wrong is actually pretty severe and the level of effort to get it right is really low, because again, in that test that we run internally, the amount of time it takes bots -- and this will improve, but at least as of today, the amount of time it takes bots to get actionable quotes back, it's actually longer than the amount of time it takes for a human agent to just write your policy and one that you're fully protected on. That agent has E&O coverage to make sure even if they miss something, in the unlikely event that they did, that you as the client aren't damaged.

So it will be an interesting and dynamic time, but we feel like we're positioned in the right spot in the value chain. We have the right relationships with our underwriters. And we have the right technology team to prepare ourselves for how the market changes.

Randy Binner: That's a good anecdote. Just to make sure I understood it correctly, so that 25% price range, I guess we'll call it on the auto quotes, was on auto. That did not include homeowners quotes. That was just auto for that activity.

Mark Jones Jr.: Correct. Yes, the bots were unable to get homeowners quotes. They were able to get auto with the same carrier, one being $1,000, one being $1,250 with all of the exact same information.

Randy Binner: Just one more, if I can. Just on pricing, where are you seeing, kind of at the midpoint across your markets, just auto and home price softening kind of year-over-year in the third quarter?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. Auto is down, call it, mid-single digits and home is down low single digits. That can be more dramatic in specific markets, places like Texas and Florida. But if you look at the policy in force growth rate of 14% compared to the premium growth rate of 11%, you can effectively get to an at-large average price decline of about 3 percentage points.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Andrew Andersen of Jefferies.

Andrew Andersen: As you expand the Digital Agent and build the MCP connection for these third-party AI assistants, should we expect any meaningful increase in technology spending? Or can that be completed within the existing cost base?

Mark Jones Jr.: We don't expect to change our previous expectations on 2027 technology spend.

Andrew Andersen: Okay. And as you talk about the product market becoming a bit more competitive, can you talk about what you're seeing in base commission rates or contingent terms and if that could help offset some of the lower premium per policy over time?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. Base commission rates are continuing to be stable to improving, and that kind of depends on the specific geography. And some of that is a function of the admitted markets being pretty significantly healed and those naturally tend to have higher commission rates. I think there's been a lot of industry data, I think even from you, specifically, Andrew, on the growth rates in E&S and how those have kind of leveled off with the healed admitted market.

And we've done a really good job working with our underwriters to determine what's the fair and right compensation for the level of growth and profitability our business is able to provide, which we believe is differentiated from the average agent, given how we go to market. So that's kind of the core commission rate point. And then on the contingency side, this was a really specific area of focus for us in 2026, just given how we anticipated the product market would heal and profitability would look for underwriters.

I think we've done a great job working with our carrier partners to understand how do we maximize value for them and then how do we get to take part in that upside. And that's going to be reflected in our contingent commissions this year. I think we previously said something like 70 to 100 basis points of contingent commission expectations for the year. I think we could probably confidently say that's more like 80 to 110 basis points of premium as contingencies for this year. And we've done a good job writing high-quality business. So the loss ratios have performed very, very well this year.

Operator: Our next question will be coming from the line of Mark Hughes of Truist.

Mark Hughes: Anything you can say about the contingent commissions outlook for the balance of the year? And any updates on those expectations?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes, Mark, I would say we're expecting contingent commissions for the full year to be between 80 and 110 basis points of total written premium. So that would reflect an improvement over our second quarter expectation. And that's a function of delivering high growth and profitable new business as well as improvements in the quality of contracts that we have.

Mark Hughes: Yes. Anything you can say, any details on just the restatement, the commissions paid to obtain customer contracts? Was there a particular component of the commissions or some category of counterparty that you're paying those commissions to that are now going to be capitalized? And I hear your point, it's going to make the P&L look even better. But what was the issue? If you could -- any detail would be appreciated.

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. It really stems from variable compensation paid to corporate sales agents in generation of new business. And obviously, I would point you back to the 8-K for the specifics on the disclosure. But ultimately, all this impact is we'll be putting more expense on the balance sheet and recognizing it over a longer period of time. Now we'll have full financial statements restated as soon as practically available. But ultimately, this results in improvements in the P&L, which is an interesting position to be in.

Mark Hughes: Is that going to impact EBITDA? Is that going to be corrected for or adjusted for?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes, we would anticipate declines in compensation expense and increases in the associated income numbers, including adjusted EBITDA by that same amount. And so if you look at the 8-K, the 2025 range that we gave, the math on that effectuates a $1 million to $11 million range with a $6 million midpoint.

Mark Hughes: Yes. So this is not an EBITDA add-back -- amortization add back?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes, it's coming right out of compensation expense. So it will result in an improvement in EBITDA.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Rowland Mayor of RBC Capital Markets.

Rowland Mayor: It sounded like you had already done the full accounting review, but do you expect there to be any incremental costs associated with the restatement process?

Mark Jones Jr.: It's hard to comment on that specifically right now. I would say we anticipate there being some portion of G&A that needs to get spent in terms of actually delivering the fully restated financial statements. I don't anticipate that being a material number.

Rowland Mayor: And then I guess on agent productivity, you showed some nice year-over-year gains in the franchise side, but corporate agents were more stable. Is that unusual?

Mark Jones Jr.: I wouldn't say it's unusual. And really, corporate agents in their first year are more impacted by the housing market than the longer tenured ones, just given they're in the process of building their referral partner network as well as we've done 48 total agents from the corporate team this year launched into other portions of the business. And that includes 19 franchises that came out of corporate that are producing at high levels, 9 producers that went to work for either embedded franchises or other existing agencies and then 20 additional producers who have gone to other productive areas of the business, including the enterprise sales team. And usually, those are some of the more productive people.

So if you think back to 1 or 2 calls ago, we were talking about the real purpose of the corporate sales team is to be a talent incubator for other portions of the organization. That is performing exactly as anticipated.

Rowland Mayor: Then if I could just get one more in. We moved through hurricane season in the quarter, and I was wondering if you started to see changes in the pricing environment as companies anticipate reinsurance price cuts next year?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. I mean the third quarter had more pricing declines in it than the second quarter did, and that may be in anticipation of reinsurance pricing coming down, although I don't have a crystal ball. And obviously, we don't have any balance sheet risk, so we're not directly exposed to reinsurance costs.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Ryan Tunis of Cantor.

Ryan Tunis: I guess I've got 3 ones on the accounting stuff. The first one, this change, I think, is going to make your noncore revenues more like 17% of total. So I'm just curious how you think about that. Now that we've got the initial franchise fees and this, should we be concerned that, like, too big of your business is being driven by your franchises reimbursing you or paying you, however you want to call it?

Mark Jones Jr.: Ryan, this has existed forever. Franchisees have paid us to access the technology that we've spent tens of millions of dollars building over our history. This is purely a geography issue inside the P&L. So we're not changing business decisions based on how the accounting works here. And we want to make sure we get the accounting right, which is why we're going through this process. But this doesn't change anything about how we manage the business. It also has no impact to cash flows or earnings, that specific technology piece.

Ryan Tunis: Appreciate it. It just changes the way you look at revenues. Second question, so ASC 606, I think, has been around since 2018. This is a 2023 and 2025 issue. Can you just give me some context on why is this not a 2022, 2021, 2019 issue? Why did this crop up in 2023?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. I would just refer you to the 8-K on the disclosures related to this topic.

Ryan Tunis: And then just lastly, I think analysts, like myself included, have found a lot of, like, margin volatility over the years. It sounds like you're capitalizing some stuff. Is it fair to assume that the margin profile should become more stable moving forward? Yes, I'll leave it there.

Mark Jones Jr.: Ryan, margins have only effectively gone in really one direction for the last 6 years -- I think, 5 or 6 years. They've effectively only gone up since the 2021 period. Now this year, we messaged specifically why you should expect margin compression. That's a result of investments into things that we believe are going to drive faster longer-term growth. And we're going to have the discipline to continue to make those trade-offs. We don't want to trade off short-term margin for long-term total profit dollars. But we are a high-growth organization. I mean we're 3x to 5x the public broker average of organic growth, depending on who you're comparing against.

And we deliver pretty strong and stable margins in the high 20s, low 30 percentage points range. And I think if you ask me, would I prefer to have revenue growth faster or margin higher, I'd prefer to have revenue growth faster. So as we look for opportunities to drive faster revenue growth, I'm happy to make that short-term margin trade-off to drive long-term market share gains.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Pablo Singzon of JPMorgan.

Pablo Singzon: Do you have a view on when the pricing pressure will abate? I think you had originally signaled -- and this might have been quite early in the year, right? But I think one of the messages was that you expect the pricing pressure to abate in the second half. So I was wondering if you had an updated view there.

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes, Pablo, I think the message was really we expected the rate of improvement of client retention to be even faster than the pricing impact. And what has happened is the pricing impact has gotten more substantial in the third quarter and not been stable relative to the second quarter, which is why you're seeing the directionality on revenue retention of renewal commissions. It's hard for me to put a stake in the ground and tell you exactly when pricing is going to level off. I think I tried to do that in '23 and in '24 and was ultimately not correct on those topics because of the general extremeness of the hard market.

We'll see as we start to lap some of these comparisons in terms of how soft this market has been. I don't necessarily anticipate underwriters are going to continue to slash prices forever. But we are at the entry point of a soft market, which means that we're probably in a downward pressure on pricing for some period of time, followed by stability and then moderate price increases, which is really a better operating environment for us to be in.

Pablo Singzon: Fair enough. And then the second question, how does the pricing pressure affect your ability to maintain or expand margins just given your ongoing investments, right? Are you seeing enough of an offset from efficiency initiatives? And I guess what I have in mind are your larger counterparts, right? Obviously, they're not growing as fast as you guys, but basically all the bigger brokers at this point have some sort of expense management plan in place. I was wondering if that's something that you might be considering.

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. I would say they're kind of 2 separate topics, right? We try to manage the business on the factors that we can control while understanding what's going on with the other factors outside of our control. And so I don't want to be making rash business decisions in our operations based on what's going on with pricing. We take a long-term outlook. We understand that, over a long period of time, pricing will effectively look one direction. It's not going to, over a long period of time, be swinging up and down. And so I don't want to be jerking the organization around. But having said that, we're always looking for opportunities to get more efficient.

And we talked about, in our prepared remarks, some of the AI initiatives associated with our service function, which have gone incredibly well. We're delivering a really excellent client service at an effectively reduced cost over the previous year just in terms of that direct measurement. And that's a function of us investing in technology that both aids our clients and aids our teammates in making their lives easier. So we're going to continue to do those kind of things as well as try and drive unit productivity. So we can control how many policies we sell. We can't control the price of what those policies are.

So we're focused on driving as much unit productivity as possible and reducing our costs wherever we can.

Operator: Our next question is coming from the line of Katie Sakys of Autonomous Research.

Katie Sakys: I had a follow up on the previous question about pricing pressures. I appreciate that you guys don't have a crystal ball on what carriers in the market are going to trend towards over the next couple of quarters or years. But I do think that you guys have a fairly decent understanding of where your productivity momentum should be trending and how your overall footprint should be changing. So just curious whether or not you expect the rate of client retention improvement and overall new business growth to be able to offset the headwinds from premium retention next year? And does that ultimately mean that we could see core revenue growth accelerate in 2027?

Mark Jones Jr.: Yes. I mean the key to driving accelerating core revenue growth rates, and obviously, I'm not going to give 2027 guidance right now, but just philosophically, the key to driving accelerated core revenue growth rate is improving client retention and accelerating new business production, particularly on the franchise side of the business, given how that mechanism goes from 20% recognition on new business to 50% on renewal. And so we've talked about 2026, we anticipate driving accelerated franchise new business production for the full year. We said that in our prepared remarks. So that's kind of point one into driving accelerated core revenue growth rates.

And we'll do everything in our power to make client retention grow as high as it can as quickly as it can. We've put our smartest AI resources against this specifically because this is where there's the largest impact in the business in terms of both revenue growth and earnings expansion. And it's also just the right thing to do for the clients, which is really how we guide all of our business decisions. But if you weigh those 2 things, we've kind of accomplished one already in driving accelerated franchise new business growth over the previous year, and we're in the process of continuously improving client retention.

And like we said previously, pricing is going to do what it's going to do. We're going to stay focused on what we can control. We're going to stay focused on our clients, and we'll execute to the best of our capabilities.

Katie Sakys: Got it. Perhaps as a follow-up, I continue to be impressed by the productivity of corporate agent-launched franchises. Given how far above their weight they continue to punch, does it make sense to expand your efforts in fostering and developing that talent and sending them out into the franchise channel rather than focusing on continuing to onboard independent agents or other franchise operators who don't come from within the Goosehead ecosystem?

Mark Jones Jr.: That's a great question, Katie. And really, it's both. So it's not either/or. Launching franchises out of the corporate business has been an incredibly successful endeavor, and I'm very happy about the direction of that. Launching franchises that we have found in the wild has gotten us to where we are today, which is a large group of very successful businesses. We said in our prepared remarks, we've got a franchise now approaching $1 million of cash flow to them from us a month. That is a pretty impressive and durable business, and we're consistently seeing pretty strong same-store sales growth in the franchise business. It's 17% overall for the third quarter and 29% in our top 50.

So we're certainly not going to abandon hunting new franchises in the wild, although the profile of who we're bringing in has changed. It's not looking the same as the profile that it was in 2018. There's less insurance-focused people coming through the top of the funnel. There's more serial entrepreneurs, people who own multiple businesses, people that have capital that are ready to deploy, people who when you're pitching them on the model, you can effectively cover up the word insurance and just show them the economic model and they go, yes, I get that, capital-light, high recurring revenue, easy to launch, underpenetrated market, good technology, all the things that we would explain in our value proposition.

So we're not going to stop doing either one of those things. They're both very value-accretive to us.

Operator: And there are no more questions in the queue. I would like to now turn the call back over to Mark Jones Jr. for closing remarks. Please go ahead.

Mark Jones Jr.: Thank you all for joining us this afternoon, and thank you for your continued support of Goosehead. We look forward to speaking to you again soon.

Operator: This concludes today's program, and thank you so much for participating. You may now disconnect.

#3257. Take-Two: 3 Key Takeaways for Long-Term Investors

Direct mobile sales let Take-Two keep fees that app stores would otherwise collect, so margin gains may matter more than quarterly bookings swings.

On its second-quarter fiscal year 2027 earnings call, held on Nov. 9, 2026, Take-Two (TTWO -3.48%) reiterated its full-year net bookings target of $8 billion to $8.2 billion despite second-quarter net bookings falling slightly short of guidance. For long-term investors, quarterly swings matter far less than the company's ability to turn huge game releases into multiyear streams of recurring player spending. Three key takeaways from management explain how that strategy is unfolding.

The scheduled release of Grand Theft Auto VI on Nov. 19, 2026, is the primary growth engine for the business. Extraordinary preorder demand gave executive leadership the confidence to keep full-year bookings targets intact despite initial softness in other titles.

Second-quarter net bookings--the total dollar value of products sold digitally or physically--landed at $1.6 billion, slightly below the guided $1.62 billion to $1.67 billion range due to a slower start for NBA 2K27. Management plans to roll out extensive post-launch content to accelerate recurring player spending in the second half of the fiscal year.

By selling mobile content directly to consumers rather than relying solely on third-party app stores, Take-Two bypasses platform distribution fees. This direct-to-consumer expansion lowers transaction costs, deepens player relationships, and protects profit margins across its mobile portfolio.

Cash flow generation is on track to meet key milestones, and management is clearly confident in its financial trajectory.

Long-term value relies on expanding global digital distribution and direct mobile sales, and on building a permanent higher baseline for recurring player revenue.

The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Take-Two Interactive Software. The Motley Fool has a disclosure policy.

#3256. Adobe puts its Coworker AI agent in GenStudio, free for existing customers

Briefs, audience checks and on-brand asset versions now start with a chat. When Brand Intelligence and a human reviewer disagree, the human makes the call, Adobe told TNW.

Adobe’s AI agent for marketing teams, CX Enterprise Coworker, is now live inside GenStudio. That is Adobe’s software for producing and delivering marketing content. Teams ask it for what they need in plain language. The agent then carries the work across Adobe’s apps and the outside tools a team already uses.

Adobe announced the launch today at its MAX conference in Miami Beach. Coworker is free for existing licensed GenStudio customers, Adobe told TNW. All the new tools are available to customers worldwide.

It works across Adobe Experience Manager, Workfront, Brand Intelligence, Frame.io and GenStudio for Performance Marketing, depending on a customer’s licences. Teams can also use it as a standalone app, or inside Experience Manager, Workfront and Adobe Content Analytics.

Adobe says Coworker can draft campaign briefs, assess target audiences and produce versions of an asset for different channels and markets. It connects to other apps through the Model Context Protocol and Agent-to-Agent, two open standards for AI agents. Earlier this month, Adobe put the same agent inside ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot.

Varun Parmar runs GenStudio and Firefly Enterprise at Adobe. He said GenStudio has delivered more than 7.8 trillion assets so far this year. Adobe told TNW the figure counts every delivery of an image, video or 3D file to a website, app or other channel through Adobe Experience Manager. One asset can count many times. GenStudio manages more than 650 million assets for its customers.

Coworker draws on Adobe Brand Intelligence, an AI that learns a brand’s standards. It learns from written guidelines and from the unwritten knowledge built up inside a company. Teams can run brand checks straight from a Coworker conversation.

TNW asked Adobe what happens when the AI and a human reviewer disagree about whether a piece is on brand. Parmar said people make the call.

“Human judgment has the final say. Brand Intelligence gives people and agents the brand context they need and checks work against brand standards at a scale no team could manage by hand, but people set the guardrails and make the call,” Parmar told TNW.

He said the system learns from every review.

“The system learns from both written guidelines and the feedback teams give during reviews in tools like Photoshop and Workfront, so every decision a reviewer makes helps it better reflect how that brand actually thinks,” he said.

Brand Intelligence also gets a new feature called intelligent asset adaptation. It resizes and rearranges a design for other formats, such as a website banner or a mobile ad. The new versions stay on brand. Adobe is building Brand Intelligence into Photoshop, Illustrator, InDesign and Firefly Creative Production for Enterprise.

Adobe backs the push with its own research, carried out by research firm Incisiv. It surveyed 607 marketing, creative and brand professionals at companies with $1 billion or more in annual revenue. It also polled 1,107 consumers and 304 business buyers in North America in July and August.

Staff closer to the work estimated that 27% of their company’s public-facing content is off-brand. Senior leaders put the figure at 9%. Adobe told TNW the gap shows how hard it is to keep to brand standards as the volume of content grows.

Of the professionals who approve content, 74% said they had signed off on off-brand work. Among those who had piloted automated brand-checking tools, 75% reported a mixed or negative experience.

In Workfront, Adobe’s project management software, a new Ideation Space gives teams a shared AI canvas. Coworker pulls past campaign results and product details onto it, and the team turns them into a structured brief. Adobe’s example is a retailer planning a Black Friday campaign.

Firefly Graph for enterprise lets teams build repeatable creative workflows from Adobe’s apps and outside AI models. Two new features are in beta. Capsules turn a finished workflow into a simple app that anyone can run, and Node Publishing lets teams build shareable custom workflow parts.

Firefly Graph outputs will also carry Content Credentials tied to the organisation, which record where an asset came from. Adobe’s 3D Digital Twin, which makes digital copies of products, can now place them in new 3D scenes. Teams and agents can also change labels and materials, generate video and set custom lighting.

Adobe has added AI to GenStudio before, and it sells its creative tools inside ChatGPT. Xfinity is bringing Coworker into how it runs campaigns.

“Bringing Adobe Coworker into how we run campaigns gives us one place to direct the work,” said Christopher Grove, vice president of GenAI and creative tech at Xfinity.

#3253. Why Lockheed Martin Rallied in October

Strong earnings, along with visibility into longer-term F-35 and missile demand, pushed shares higher.

Shares of Lockheed Martin (LMT +3.72%) rallied 25.1% in October, according to data from S&P Global Market Intelligence.

The largest defense contractor rallied on the back of strong third-quarter earnings last month. On top of the strong results, the company closed longer-term deals with the Department of Defense, earning increased confidence from the analyst community.

In the third quarter, Lockheed saw its revenue rise 11.3% to $20.7 billion, while diluted earnings per share grew 14.6% to $7.95. Both figures handily beat analyst expectations. Management also raised its full-year guidance to a revenue range of $80 billion to $82 billion, up by $250 million on both ends, and diluted EPS to a range of $30.35 to $30.75, up from $29.95 to $30.65 previously.

Lockheed benefited from strong growth in its Aeronautics division, which produces the F-35 fighter jet, and Missiles and Fire Control, which is seeing outsize growth due to missile use in the war in Iran and the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Aeronautics rallied 13.2%, while Missiles and Fire Control grew 24.2%.

Management also announced that the Department of Defense had finalized a 10-year agreement for F-35s, with a minimum of 850 aircraft to be sold over the period, and Lockheed guaranteeing a production capacity of 156 aircraft per year. Guaranteeing a sales floor will enable Lockheed to fund the expansion itself, which should, in theory, reduce or delay government outlays. Lockheed also signed another agreement with the Department of Defense to accelerate production of the Joint Advanced Tactical Missile.

The long-term agreements were perhaps even a bigger deal than earnings results themselves. After earnings, Morgan Stanley analyst Kristine Liwag raised her price target on the stock from $690 to $835 per share. Liwag believes the long-term agreements not only boost Lockheed’s revenue outlook but also reduce the risk of future cash flows, justifying her big jump in valuation.

Buoyed by the F-35 program and with a strong growth outlook for its missile business, to say nothing of its other segments, including the Space division and Lockheed’s famous Skunk Works research and development operation, the 2.5% dividend-yielding Lockheed Martin is the premier blue chip defense contractor to own in long-term portfolios.

While the new Congress may add to uncertainty, the biggest defense stock in the market appears to be shrugging that off for now in the wake of these new long-term agreements.

#3252. MagSafe Monday: Pelican’s MagSafe wallet is built for the people who still carry cash

I’ve been on a Pelican kick this fall. It started with the Pelican MagSafe Wallet, then the Pelican MagSafe Battery Pack, and the reason is pretty simple: once the weather turns cool, I want iPhone accessories built for the outdoors because I am outside more. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is really helpful is you want something rugged, but also supports holding cash.

MagSafe Monday: Every Monday, Bradley Chambers looks at the latest and greatest in the MagSafe and wireless charging industry to help you get the most out of your Apple devices that support wireless charging.

Most magnetic wallets are a simple card sleeve and nothing else. If you carry a few $5 bills for tips, cash-only places, etc., you end up folding them around a card and hoping they don’t slip out. The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet has a stainless steel money clip on the outside of the wallet, so the cash rides on the back, where you can access it without pulling your credit cards out. It’s the same hard-shell construction as the rest of Pelican’s lineup, with the same MagSafe magnets.

The wallet holds up to five cards, which is just about perfect for my use cases. That covers my Driver’s license, debit card, and a few credit cards. There are ridges inside that push the cards up when you squeeze, so you’re not digging with your nails. A steel plate blocks RFID scanning, and the shell is rated IPX4 for water, which covers rain, etc.

Pelican calls its drop protection military-grade, which is what every accessory company says. A more useful way to think about it is that it’s a hard-shell wallet rather than a leather or silicone one.

Two things to know going in with this wallet. Five cards plus a clip of cash makes for a thick back on your phone, so this isn’t a very slim wallet. If you’re replacing a money clip, you are basically combining the two into one.

If you never carry much cash, the original Pelican wallet is the better pick. If you do want to carry a bunch of cash, the Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is an awesome pickup.

The Pelican Protector Magnetic Money Clip Wallet is available on Amazon and directly from Pelican.

#3251. This Growth ETF Has Crushed the S&P 500 Since 2004. Here's Why It's Still a Buy.

The upside outweighs the inevitable volatility.

For a growth investor, the goal of any investment, whether an individual stock or ETF, should be to grow as much as possible. However, when it comes to comparisons, the S&P 500 (^GSPC +2.35%) remains the benchmark for measuring performance.

One ETF that has routinely outperformed the S&P 500 since it began trading in January 2004 is the Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG +2.77%). In that time, it's up 895% compared to the S&P 500's 539%. Only time will tell what the future holds, but signs point to that trend continuing.

VUG holds 135 large-cap growth stocks across all major sectors, but it's heavily concentrated in tech (72.1%). That checks out given its growth focus, but it also helps to have a hedge in other sectors. All of its top 10 holdings are tech companies (including the "Magnificent Seven" stocks), but its top 20 includes blue chip stocks like Eli Lilly, Visa, Mastercard, and Costco Wholesale.

The high concentration in tech means when it's good, it's great, but when it's bad, it can be terrible. Luckily, it's been much more on the great side. Here's how its returns compare to the S&P 500's over different time spans:

Source: YCharts. Averages as of market close on Nov. 6.

With VUG down 11% in the past month, and the Nasdaq Composite officially in correction territory as of market close on Nov. 6, investors may wonder whether now's the time to invest, with bear market fears looming and uncertainty high.

While we can't predict how the market will move (particularly in the short term), I trust VUG to weather the storm. It has experienced three bear markets -- the financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, and the 2022 bear market -- and bounced back from each:

Data source: YCharts. Returns are based on VUG's $82.17 closing price on Nov. 6. Percentages rounded to the nearest whole percent.

Past results don't guarantee future performance, so we can't assume it will continue. However, the companies leading the way in VUG are built to succeed over the long haul. That doesn't mean there won't be hiccups and rough patches along the way (there absolutely will be), but the long-term trajectory matters much more than the short-term surges or plunges.

I wouldn't invest a lump sum in VUG right now because of the volatility, but it's a good time to start a stake or slowly add to an existing position.

This iPhone app provides contactless sleep tracking, and it holds its own against my gold-standard Oura Ring 5

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I've been tracking my sleep with the Oura Ring 5 for the past five months and love its comfortable fit and reliable data, whether I’m monitoring my 3 a.m. wake ups or how long I spend in deep sleep. However, the Oura Ring 5, now from $399 at Amazon, does come at a premium price. Keen to see if it was possible to replicate the accuracy of the Oura without the high cost, I started testing free sleep tracking apps — and discovered one that could hold its own against the best sleep tracker we’ve tested, the Oura Ring 5. The good news? It's completely free, with no hidden costs or trial sign-ups; all you need is a smart phone and a nightstand.

Here's how this free iPhone app compares to my $499 Oura Ring 5 (the gold costs more), plus how I'm using its tracking data to better understand my sleep. Looking for a wearable sleep tracker instead? I've rounded up the top sleep trackers you can buy in this year's Black Friday sleep sales, too.

There are plenty of free sleep tracking apps out there, so I decided to test three popular ones against my Oura Ring 5. The Oura Ring 5 is a luxury smart ring with highly-sophisticated sensor technology that can monitor your sleep cycles, sleep duration, and sleep latency (in other words, how long it takes you to fall asleep).

So, not only I was looking a free app that could provide those metrics, I was looking for a free app that could provide those metrics accurately.

After the Sleep Cycle and SleepScore apps failed to dazzle me, I didn't hold out much hope for the Sleepwave app, which you can get for free at the App store. Still, a 4.6 star rating out of 5 from over 3,700 user reviews convinced me to give the self-proclaimed "best free sleep tracker app" a go.

The Sleepwave app is completely contactless; you simply put your iPhone on your nightstand or mattress. Its sleep tracking relies mostly on movements (for example, from tossing and turning) and breathing, which are picked up by patented motion-sensing technology, as Sleepwave maintains that motion indicates wakefulness.

When I woke up after using the app for the first time, my expectations were low. However, comparing the Sleepwave's sleep data to my Oura Ring 5's, I was blown away by the accuracy of its metrics. From my overall sleep duration, my time spent awake during the night (including how long my 3 a.m. wake ups lasted), my sleep stages, and sleep latency.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The metrics are all presented in a bright infographic format, which is easy to read. On top of these sleep metrics, the Sleepwave app also includes a smart alarm which wakes you up during light sleep in the morning (when you're naturally more inclined to wake up), so it feels less jarring than being awoken during deep sleep.

Plus, thanks to the iPhone's microphone, you can listen to recordings of your bedroom's nocturnal noises, including snoring, vehicles, or pets — handy if you're a light sleeper like me who wants to see whether it's noise that is waking you up at 3 a.m.

As mentioned above, I tested the Sleepwave's accuracy by using the app while wearing my Oura Ring 5 and then comparing the data the next morning.

Here's a comparison between data from the Oura Ring and the Sleepwave app, recorded on the same night:

I consider a result 5 minutes under or over the Oura Ring metrics as an accurate match. As you can see from the above table, all metrics (apart from the REM sleep metric) fell within the 5-minute threshold — a remarkable result from a free sleep tracker app that's up against a $499 smart ring.

Of course, there things that the Oura Ring can do that the Sleepwave can't. For instance, the Sleepwave doesn't provide a readiness score (which tells you how much your sleep quality has prepared you for the day), heart rate variability (HRV), a sleep chronotype (your natural circadian rhythm), and health and fitness readings.

Still, if your main goal is to understand how long you fall asleep for or how much deep sleep you're racking up, then I highly reccomend giving the Sleepwave app a try (I mean, it's free, so what have you got to lose?).

The Oura Ring 4 may have been usurped by 2026's Oura Ring 5, but it still shares plenty of the same lab-accurate sleep tracking features with its successor. Right now, you'll find discounts on the metallic finishes (such as Silver and Black), which are down to $249. A Gold finish, meanwhile, will set you back $279.99...but it is down from $399.99. As with the Oura Ring 5, you'll need to pay a monthly subscription of $5.99.

The Garmin Index Sleep Monitor is a comfortable armband from the brand best known for GPS systems and sports watches. We were impressed with its accurate sleep data and lightweight sleep comfort, but it's not a great investment if you want fitness tracking, too. You'll find the Index Sleep Monitor for $169.99 at Amazon, though we have seen discounts during holiday sales like Cyber Monday.

If you're looking for both sleep and fitness tracking (like the Oura Ring) but want something more affordable, then the subscription-free Fitbit Air offers fuss-free, all-round tracking. It provides detailed sleep reports for under $100 and its app is intuitive to use, too. However, be aware that its strap can feel a little bulky to wear to bed at night.
