#3248. Prediction: Nov. 17 Will Be a Huge Day for the Stock Market

Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17.

Nov. 17 could be one of the most important dates remaining on Wall Street's 2026 calendar. That's when Nvidia (NVDA -4.27%) is scheduled to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 earnings, giving investors an opportunity to assess the strength of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution.

The timing is particularly interesting. Technology stocks have experienced considerable volatility amid concerns about AI infrastructure spending, potential regulation, and whether the industry's growth is sustainable.

Meanwhile, Nvidia is facing additional scrutiny surrounding CEO Jensen Huang, introducing uncertainty about the company's leadership. I think investors should be focusing on what Nvidia's upcoming earnings reveal about the underlying business. Based on management's latest guidance, there's reason to believe the growth story remains intact.

During the company's fiscal second quarter (ended July 26), Nvidia generated $96.2 billion in revenue, representing a 106% increase year over year. Data center revenue reached $89 billion, increasing 117% annually. Meanwhile, earnings per share (EPS) climbed 128% to $2.46, while the company's gross margin reached 75%.

What's even more encouraging is the company expects more growth. Management guided for $108 billion in third-quarter revenue, plus or minus 2%, representing roughly 89% growth compared with the same quarter last year.

Wall Street's expectations are slightly higher. Analysts are projecting approximately $108.9 billion in revenue and EPS of $2.47. That would represent roughly 91% revenue growth and 90% earnings growth year over year. Importantly, Nvidia's guidance does not assume any data center revenue from China.

Nvidia's growth isn't just the result of companies experimenting with AI. The company is heavily embedded with capital expenditure (capex) commitments from cloud computing providers, frontier model developers, and enterprises building production-scale applications.

Companies including Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet, Meta Platforms, Oracle, Anthropic, and OpenAI are expanding their data center footprints to support AI training and inference. These investments translate directly into demand for Nvidia's GPUs, networking equipment, and integrated computing systems.

The company's Blackwell architecture is an important component of hyperscaler infrastructure, supporting AI training and inference workloads. Meanwhile, Nvidia's new Vera Rubin platform is in full production, with deployments underway across cloud providers including Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and CoreWeave.

Rubin combines GPU computing with Nvidia's Vera CPUs and high-speed networking systems. Training generative models requires enormous levels of compute. However, inference -- the process of generating responses and performing tasks using trained models -- is now also becoming a major source of computing demand.

As AI applications become more sophisticated, the amount of compute required to serve end users will increase substantially. Nvidia is positioning its GPUs, CPUs, networking systems, and CUDA software to capture more spending across various layers of AI workloads.

Beyond Nvidia's financial results, investors are navigating a new source of uncertainty. Nvidia's board of directors recently launched an independent investigation following reports that Huang had a relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence. Huang has acknowledged an extramarital affair, while the intelligence allegations remain under investigation and Nvidia says it has no reason to believe trade secrets were compromised.

The development has weighed on investor sentiment, particularly because Huang has played such a central role in Nvidia's growth. However, investors should not confuse questions surrounding corporate leadership with evidence that demand for Nvidia's products is going away. Those are separate issues.

I'll be watching three things particularly closely: data center revenue growth, gross margin, and management's fourth-quarter outlook. If Nvidia delivers another strong quarter but offers disappointing guidance, investors could interpret that as evidence that AI infrastructure spending is beginning to moderate. Conversely, results that exceed expectations alongside accelerating demand for Vera Rubin could help restore confidence in the company's growth trajectory.

Of course, even a blowout earnings report will not automatically resolve the governance investigation, and a strong report does not guarantee an immediate stock price recovery. Given Nvidia's importance to the broader AI trade, the implications could extend well beyond a single semiconductor stock.

Still, I think the company's underlying financial performance deserves considerably more attention than the short-term narrative described in headlines. This is why I expect Nov. 17 to be a significant day for the entire stock market.

Netflix's top 10 shows list is always changing, which can make it tricky to know what’s actually worth adding to your watchlist. But if you’re anything like me, you don’t always have time to sift through dozens of titles to find your next binge-watch.

So, I’ve taken a look at what’s currently trending on Netflix and picked out three shows that deserve your attention this week. Whether you’re after a twist-filled spy thriller about a secret agent, a warm-hearted comedy set in a small Arctic community, or a gripping prison drama, there’s something here for you. Note: This list is based on the Netflix U.S. top 10 shows as of Tuesday, November 10, 2026.

The second season of “Black Doves” is here, which means you have six new episodes to binge-watch this week. Originally planned as a limited series, the spy thriller proved popular enough to earn a second outing, with creator Joe Barton and production company Sister returning for another chapter. I’d also argue it deserves a place among this year’s Christmas viewing, thanks to its wintry London backdrop, complete with sparkling festive displays and freezing streets. The story itself is far from cozy, but that contrast makes it an interesting choice for the holiday season.

Helen Webb (Keira Knightley) leads a double life as an undercover spy for a secretive organization that sells stolen intelligence to the highest bidder. Director Anya Adams, whose credits include “Yellowjackets” and “Abbott Elementary,” helps bring plenty of personality to the ensemble. With the show already making an appearance in Netflix’s top 10, there’s plenty of reason to give this one a try.

Siaja (Anna Lambe) is a young Inuk mother who makes a very public exit from her marriage and attempts to start afresh with her young daughter in the small Arctic town of Ice Cove, Nunavut. Stream "North of North" season 2 on Netflix

The series was the first fully owned original scripted drama developed for SundanceTV and ran for four seasons, with 30 episodes in total. Key signs of a healthy plant that will last all season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Now that I’ve flipped my calendar to November, I’m counting down to Christmas and planning how I’ll decorate my home.

However, I don’t stick to the usual festive tree and decorative lights; I always rely on seasonal houseplants to bring vibrant life into the mix. Apart from my Christmas cactus, a poinsettia is a must-have — it’s basically Christmas in a pot.

Step into any garden center in mid-November, and you can’t miss a sea of crimson. Poinsettias have officially arrived and are the bright spark of color that signals the holiday season is near. But picking up a pot before Santa slides down the chimney comes with a risk. Choose the wrong plant now, and you could be left with a wilted stem by Christmas morning.

So how do you choose the perfect poinsettia so it still looks good when Santa arrives in December? Here, David Denyer, flower expert at Eflorist, shares how to choose a poinsettia in November so it creates a perfect display right through to the New Year.

Whether you’re picking a poinsettia for yourself or as a festive gift, Denyer advises checking the center of the colored leaves, known as bracts. “You’ll see small yellow-green buds, which are the true flowers. If these are still tight and unopened, your plant is fresh and will last much longer.”

Did you know?The colored sections on a poinsettia look like flowers, but they’re bracts, often called modified leaves. The red ‘petals’ have developed to attract pollinators to the tiny flowers in the center. Bougainvilleas and passion flowers are two other plants with bracts that are easy to mistake for petals.

When you go to buy a poinsettia, Denyer says there are two red flags to watch for. He advises against buying a poinsettia with drooping, yellowing or missing leaves. It’s not a healthy start.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

There’s another danger sign to watch for before buying this festive plant. Denyer adds, “Don’t choose plants that have been displayed outside shops or near automatic doors,” and he adds, “they’ll most likely be damaged by the cold draughts already.”

It appears that poinsettias prefer to be snug rather than chilly, so to keep your poinsettia protected, Denyer recommends, “Be sure to keep your poinsettias warm by wrapping them for the journey home; they really don’t like the cold.”

Once you’ve picked a healthy poinsettia, it needs to be treated just right to keep it looking its best, which is why it helps to know that this plant is used to sunny climates.

“Being native to Mexico, it makes sense that poinsettias love warmth and light, so placement is crucial,” says Denyer. “Select a bright room, ideally near a window where it can enjoy plenty of indirect light, but without its leaves touching the cold glass.”

They thrive in temperatures between 59-70°F (15–21°C), but they don’t like sudden changes, so he says, keep them away from draughty doorways, radiators, fireplaces and open windows, as they’ll struggle otherwise.

This attractive indoor watering can holds 35 oz of water and comes in sage green with a decorative wooden handle and a gooseneck spout. The durable stainless steel is leakproof, scratch resistant, and anti-corrosive.

According to Denyer a poinsettia will hold onto its color for at least six to eight weeks, so a plant brought in mid-November should see you through until the end of December. If you wait until December to buy your plant, it will keep going until the end of January.

There are four main stages can help you keep a poinsettia alive beyond the festive season. Here, Denyer explains what to do and when.

Late winterOnce the bracts begin to fade, gradually reduce watering and let the compost dry out a little more between drinks.

AprilCut the stems back to around 4 inches (10 cm) and keep the plant somewhere warm and bright.

MayWhen new growth appears, repot into fresh compost, then water regularly and feed every couple of weeks throughout summer.

FallFrom late September, give your plant around 14 hours of complete darkness each night for eight weeks. Covering it with a box or popping it in a cupboard overnight will do the trick. This short-day treatment triggers the colorful bracts to develop in time for Christmas.

Today Apple released iOS 27.2.1 for iPhone with bug fixes and security updates, alongside a variety of related software updates on other platforms. Here are the security fix details for each update.

Apple has just detailed all the latest security fixes included in today’s new software updates.

iOS 27.2.1 and many other updates include fixes that relate to Messages, AirPlay, Bluetooth, and more. #3237. Interactive Brokers Group vs. Nu: Which Financial Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

Nu's revenue grew about 43% in 2025, yet its forward P/E sits near 13.5 versus Interactive Brokers' 26.9, a gap that may shape which stock looks more attractive heading into 2027.

Investors seeking growth in the financial landscape often weigh established global platforms against disruptive digital leaders. Choosing between Interactive Brokers Group (IBKR +2.31%) and Nu (NU +2.74%) depends on your specific goals.

Interactive Brokers Group serves professional and active traders worldwide with sophisticated, automated tools. Nu, meanwhile, is revolutionizing banking in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia through its digital-first platform. Both companies occupy distinct niches, providing different avenues for long-term growth and geographic diversification.

Interactive Brokers Group operates an automated global electronic brokerage providing direct-access trade execution and clearing services. It serves roughly 5.5 million client accounts, including hedge funds, mutual funds, and individual investors, across 175 market centers in 40 countries. This brokerage giant is a staple among financial stocks due to its global reach and low customer concentration, with no single client representing more than 2% of commissions.

In its latest annual report, filed for fiscal 2025, Interactive Brokers reported that revenue reached nearly $6.2 billion. This represents approximately 19.7% growth compared to the prior year. Net income was close to $984 million, resulting in a net margin of roughly 15.9%, which reflects the company's ability to keep more of each dollar earned after all expenses are paid.

As of Interactive Brokers' December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio, which measures total debt relative to shareholders' equity, is approximately 0. The current ratio, which gauges the ability to cover short-term liabilities with short-term assets, stands at roughly 1.1. For fiscal 2025, free cash flow reached nearly $15.7 billion, which is calculated as cash flow from operations minus capital expenditures.

Nu is a leading digital financial services company serving approximately 131 million customers globally through its mobile-centric platform. By eliminating physical branches and traditional fees, it has become one of the most prominent fintech stocks in the Latin American market. The company focuses on expanding its user base in Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia by offering simplified credit cards, savings accounts, and personal loans.

In its latest annual report, filed for fiscal 2025, revenue reached close to $15.9 billion. This marks roughly 43% year-over-year growth, as more users joined the platform and increased their engagement. Net income was approximately $2.9 billion, while the net margin improved to about 18.1%, indicating a strong ability to convert revenue into actual profit.

As of Nu's December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is roughly 0.5. The current ratio stands at approximately 0.6. For fiscal 2025, free cash flow was nearly $3.5 billion.

Interactive Brokers Group faces intense competition from various companies, including prime brokers, online brokers, and zero-commission platforms like Robinhood Markets (HOOD +2.98%). Regulatory and legal risks are significant, as the company must comply with complex requirements from multiple domestic and foreign regulators. Technology-related risks include potential system failures or cyberattacks, while counterparty risk remains a concern, since customer defaults on margin loans could lead to substantial losses.

Nu faces competition from established regional banks and other digital entrants in the Latin American market. Economic volatility and currency fluctuations in its primary markets of Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia can significantly impact its loan portfolio and reported earnings. Furthermore, the company must manage credit risk, as an economic downturn in these regions could lead to higher default rates among its massive retail customer base.

Nu appears more attractively valued based on its lower forward P/E, while Interactive Brokers Group commands a premium for its specialized global platform.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

The P/B ratio compares the stock price with the company's book value (its assets minus its liabilities, roughly what shareholders would own on paper), and investors lean on it for insurers and banks. A lower P/B ratio means the stock costs less relative to book value.

Nu is posting strong revenue growth, but that's what I would expect for a company in the relatively early stages of its life cycle (Nu went public not even five years ago). That said, I think Interactive Brokers' revenue gains are respectable, and both companies have decent net margins.

The one knock I have against Nu is that it is a newer company and inherently riskier as a result. Plus, it operates in markets where there's greater economic volatility. I tend to be a more conservative investor, only occasionally buying spicy, high-growth stocks.

Then there's the two stocks' performance:

Since going public, Nu's returns have only slightly outpaced inflation, and the stock has massively lagged shares of Interactive Brokers. Nu hasn't beat the S&P 500, either. Of course, past performance is no indication of future results.

I think the better buy comes down to how comfortable you are with risk. Nu has all the hallmarks of a high-risk, high-reward stock, and that may appeal to some investors. But I'd prefer adding Interactive Brokers to my portfolio.

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

I won a medium fries by defeating a sinister robot that looked suspiciously similar to a McDonald’s french fry container.

Wendy’s has turned its red-headed mascot into a wisecracking warrior who battles evil french fry robots in a free mobile game called WendyQuest. The company announced the retro-style role-playing game on Nov. 4. The announcement came with a promotion where you can win codes in the game, which are redeemable for menu items like fries and burgers at Wendy’s locations.

WendyQuest is available to download on iOS and Android. Desktop users can get it through the Steam platform. Anyone can play the game, but the promotion is restricted to people who are 18 and up living in the US.

You need to sign up for a Wendy’s account to redeem a code. While the food you can win is free, it requires you to buy something when you go.

“Wendy’s has been a part of gaming culture for years, including on Twitch, Fortnite and Feast of Legends, but WendyQuest is the brand’s first fully owned video game,” a spokesperson for Wendy’s said.

In 2019, Wendy’s partnered with the online multiplayer video game Fortnite, as well as the video-streaming platform Twitch, for various promotions featuring the company’s mascot. The company even released a rule book for a traditional tabletop roleplaying game the same year, called Feast of Legends, as a free download.

I downloaded WendyQuest, and my daughter and I played it for a while. The blocky graphics are reminiscent of the home-console video games of the late 1980s and early 1990s. It plays a lot like a simplified version of the DragonQuest, Final Fantasy and Breath of Fire games from the era, only stuffed with fast-food branding.

Rather than the regular turn-based battles that come standard in the early RPGs, this game adds a timing element, where you need to press a button at the right time like you do in old golfing video games.

It’s not a bad game. The light humor is suitable for younger players, and it’s fun to play. Like many RPGs, you battle monsters to gain levels, search around the maps for hidden areas, buy items and talk to people in towns to figure out what’s going on.

It took us over an hour to complete the first region, Fryshire, and get the Fry Stone, which unlocks a promo code for medium fries, free with a purchase. But again, you have to sign up for a Wendy’s account on their website or on the company’s mobile app.

Video games have a long history of offering real-world prizes to players as promotions. Swordquest, a series of video games released in the early 1980s for the Atari 2600, famously held a contest where players tried to win actual treasure made of gold and jewels.

In 2015, a promotion for the video game Just Cause 3 offered players the chance to win a private island. Developer Square Enix clarified that it couldn’t guarantee that the island would be livable and that the winner would have to pay all the taxes involved.

The reward codes from WendyQuest expire seven days after you get them, and Wendy’s says the codes are first come, first served.

#3235. Report: Apple saved over $5 billion in taxes through Singapore and Ireland in 2026

A new Financial Times report reveals how Apple saved billions in taxes in 2026 by shifting profits through Singapore and Ireland. Here are the details.

A few days ago, Apple published its annual Form 10-K, as required by the SEC, containing detailed information about its financial performance and operations for its 2026 fiscal year.

Included in the form, as the FT noted, is information regarding how Apple reduced its tax bill by billions of dollars through its operations in Singapore and Ireland.

For years, Apple’s tax arrangements in Ireland were the subject of scrutiny, culminating in a 2024 ruling by the EU’s top court that required the company to pay €13 billion in back taxes. Apple completed the payment in 2025.

That came a few years after Apple announced plans to bring most of its $252 billion in overseas cash back to the US, following tax reforms introduced during Donald Trump’s first administration.

Since then, to discourage companies from shifting profits to countries with lower tax rates, more than 130 countries have agreed to introduce a minimum corporate tax rate of 15% for large multinational companies, as part of a 2021 initiative coordinated by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).

Under the agreement, companies that pay less than 15% in a particular country may face additional taxes to make up the difference. The new rules also resulted in an additional $2.5 billion in taxes for Apple in Singapore in 2026, according to the company’s SEC filing.

Ireland adopted the new rules in 2024, followed by Singapore in 2025.

Back to the FT’s report, it notes that new US accounting rules now require publicly traded companies to disclose when their taxes on overseas profits differ significantly from the 21% US federal corporate tax rate.

These new requirements revealed that Apple saved $2.7 billion in taxes through Singapore in 2026, surpassing the $2.6 billion it saved through Ireland.

If Apple had been taxed on all of its global profits in 2026 at the US federal rate, it would have incurred a total bill of $33bn — demonstrating the scale of the $5bn tax reduction it received from booking profits in Ireland and Singapore. The company incurred corporation taxes totalling $27bn this year.

The FT also noted that Apple’s effective tax rate in Singapore fluctuated around 10% between 2023 and 2025, but is expected to approach 15% under the new rules. Singapore’s standard corporate tax rate is 17%.

Nvidia on Sunday said it’s opening an investigation into whether Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive officer and founder, was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort after Huang admitted having an affair with a business executive who was reportedly a Chinese spy.

The announcement of any investigation follows a series of reports that Huang had developed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, who is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company that buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell computing power to Chinese AI labs.

The New York Times reported in late October that US intelligence agencies had Alice Huang under electronic surveillance for allegedly facilitating the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law. A committee of independent directors, working with outside counsel, will oversee the investigation, the board said in a statement. The company added that it “has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025.  But reports show that there are still illegal operations underway to smuggle banned chips from the US to China.

In his own memo to Nvidia employees, Huang said he was “deeply sorry” for the affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife,” he wrote. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did.” Huang, 63, added that he will cooperate fully with the board’s investigation.

The company had previously characterized Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

#3229. Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Chatbots can skew election-related information and act as an intervening layer in a voter's search.

Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.

Also: Tired of AI Overviews? I found 9 Google Search alternatives

In a new study, Yale researchers found that a third of users asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate. Grok often recommended candidates on its own without any information from users, while ChatGPT recommended candidates most often overall, and twice as much as Claude.

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).

Also: How to keep your chatbot conversations as private as possible

In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.

When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.

Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.

“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.

“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.

Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

#3228. How Smart Glasses Detector Apps Work, and How Much You Can Trust Them

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Detector apps can identify Meta’s glasses and similar devices by their Bluetooth signals, as long as they’re switched on, nearby and broadcasting.

Bluetooth devices announce themselves to nearby phones with short broadcast signals, which is how your earbuds show up when you open your phone’s Bluetooth menu. Smart glasses do the same thing, and apps such as Zuckoff listen for signals that match known models, then send an alert when one turns up nearby.

It’s a clever workaround for glasses designed to blend in. How useful it is depends on what you want it to tell you: The app can detect that a pair is close by, but not whether it’s recording. Still, that’s more notice than most people get today, especially if they haven’t spotted the glasses’ built-in LED indicator

Here’s how those apps work, what they reliably catch and what they miss.

Zuckoff, whose name takes a direct jab at Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, has joined a small ecosystem of apps such as Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner and Nearby Glasses that offer similar functionality — letting you know when someone has smart glasses activated and how close the device is, although they can’t tell you specifically whether someone is actively recording or using AI to pull up information. The apps detect approximate device proximity by sweeping local Bluetooth frequencies to locate vendor IDs, system identifiers and hardware signatures associated with smart glasses.

As Zuckoff’s website notes: “Glasses advertise loudest while powering on, pairing or leaving the case. Once paired to their owner’s phone, they can go quiet, so silence is not proof that nobody is recording, and a detection is not proof that anyone is. Signal strength gives a rough distance and no direction at all.”

Zuckoff’s developer, Pawel Szydlowski, said he was already working on projects that used Bluetooth to detect nearby devices and discovered the tech could be applied to smart glasses. “It’s just the same technology wrapped in a different paper,” he said in a video chat with CNET.

Recent reports have shown that smart glasses are being used for everything from bullying in schools to viral videos with unwitting subjects who don’t know they’re being recorded.

Since it launched in early August, the Zuckoff app has gotten 2,000 sign-ups, and Szydlowski is beta-testing an Android version he hopes to make available on the Google Play Store. The app also has a premium version for $10 a year that can run continuous detection checks in the background when the app isn’t in use.

But a booming ecosystem of DIY modifications and third-party hardware hacks is also giving smart glasses wearers unprecedented stealth by allowing them to disable the activation lights, either by bypassing the capture LEDs or by patching software to suppress system notifications.

Tech journalist Joanna Stern hosted a video showing the process in which a local hacker removed the LED light from her Ray-Ban Meta glasses for $100, allowing the wearables to secretly record without notice.

Detecting active smart glasses in public or private spaces adds a new layer of security awareness, but it raises an obvious dilemma: What do you actually do with that information? Once a detector app alerts us that smart glasses are nearby, it seems our only choices are to either leave the space or ask the wearer to remove the glasses.

Uttara Ananthakrishnan, an associate professor of information systems at the University of Washington who studies the societal impacts of technology, says we’re still figuring out the social norms around wearables like smart glasses. It’s impossible to know whether the person filming will behave responsibly, and the question of consent gets even thornier if children might be captured on video or in photos.

“Until we develop clear mechanisms to balance seamless innovation with consent, these devices will continue to turn everyday public spaces into zones of surveillance anxiety,” she said.

The Even G2 smart glasses don’t have a camera for recording photos or videos. They can pair with a separately sold R1 control ring that works as a fitness tracker.

For instance, Even Realities’ G2 smart glasses don’t include a front-facing camera at all. Instead, the Even G2 devices, released in late 2025, focus on providing the wearer with information and acting more like a personal assistant.

“We made the decision from the beginning that smart glasses don’t need to have cameras on them in order to be useful,” Even Realities CEO Will Wang told CNET in an email. “We believe something worn on your face should respect not only the person wearing it, but everyone around them.”

The G2 devices don’t record externally, a design choice Wang said gave the company a unique challenge. “Leaving the camera out also pushed us to think differently about what actually makes smart glasses useful day to day, rather than assuming more sensors automatically make a better product,” he said.

Wang said there’s room in the smart glasses market for different approaches to features and functionality, and that buyers may want to make trade-offs for devices they’ll wear on their faces. But Wang noted that the rise of smart glasses detectors indicates that social acceptance is an issue the industry needs to consider.

Over the last several months, smart glasses have been getting cheaper. And with more models and companies jumping into the fray, the demand for surveillance detectors is likely to grow — that is, unless Big Tech and wearable companies radically change their devices to make them invisible to detector apps.

Szydlowski said his hope is that, in time, Zuckoff won’t be needed at all. He pointed out that the ability to detect nearby Apple AirTag devices eventually became part of the operating systems on iOS and Android devices. If consumers pressure manufacturers and their governments to make smart glasses easier to detect, it would be “the perfect solution” to make his app obsolete, he said.

A slow-draining or completely blocked kitchen drain is a major frustration you don’t need. Besides smelling unpleasant and potentially damaging your pipes, it slows you down as you wait for your sink to empty.

Over time, warm fats, cooking oils and butter innocently slip down the drain, but instead of fully descending, they cool and solidify. Before long, that solid grease is catching hold of other small morsels of food, stopping them from making a clear escape.

But before you try to clear your blocked kitchen drain with a harsh chemical cleaner or call in a plumber, there’s an alternative method you can try.

Cleaning expert Lynsey Crombie, known as the Queen of Clean, recommends using a cooking staple to remove grease from kitchen drains. While this common ingredient is used to season food, it also dissolves grease.

And she adds, “Salt absorbs grease and liquid, lifts stubborn stains (even red wine), and is mildly antibacterial — making it perfect for soaking kitchen sponges or scrubbing chopping boards.”

In the social post, she shows herself pouring table salt down her kitchen drain, then boiling water.

A post shared by Lynsey Queen Of Clean (@lynsey_queenofclean)

This cleaning method is also recommended by Ato Energy, which shares on its blog how much salt to use. After removing the standing water from your sink, it says, “Pour about half a cup of table salt down the drain before pouring in the hot water. Let it sit for a few minutes, and then flush with hot water to clear the mixture.”

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

This flexible tool is designed to unclog drains by reaching 18 inches inside your drain. Once inserted, it can spin 360° to wrap around hair and other gunk before being removed. The set includes 5 disposable wand sticks for easy use, which can be attached to the removable handle.

For general maintenance and to keep your kitchen drain smelling fresh and free-flowing, Ato Energy suggests using vinegar and baking soda.

It suggests removing any standing water before pouring about a cup of baking soda into the drain. Then, follow with an equal amount of white or apple cider vinegar.

“The solution will bubble. That’s good! It means the chemical reaction is working,” it says.

Then, once the bubbles subside, it says to place a stopper on the drain and wait 15 minutes. You can then finish by running hot water down the drain to see if the clog has cleared. If there’s still a blockage, it advises repeating the above steps.

To avoid future blockages, ATCO Energy advises, “You can avoid tough clogs by watching what you pour down your sink. Never put bacon grease, coffee grounds or oils down your kitchen drain.”

#3224. Sundar Pichai Just Delivered Stunning News About Google Cloud

Alphabet's cloud business is growing fast, becoming more profitable, and sitting on $561 billion in contracts that haven't yet converted to revenue.

Alphabet (GOOGL +1.18%) (GOOG +0.73%) is arguably best known for its internet search and digital advertising business. Its dominance is one of the primary reasons I identified Alphabet as my top "Magnificent Seven" stock to buy at the beginning of the year.

Google Cloud has always been an important part of the business, but it wasn't the main attraction. Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing that equation.

During Alphabet's third-quarter earnings call, CEO Sundar Pichai revealed that Google Cloud revenue surged 103% year over year. "Our AI infrastructure and solutions are the major drivers for Cloud growth and our customers see us as the leading provider here, so there's huge demand," he said.

That's an impressive number for a business operating at Google's scale. And it raises an interesting question for investors: Could Google Cloud become an even bigger reason to own Alphabet stock?

Alphabet CEO Sundar Pichai. Image source: Alphabet.

Alphabet reported Google Cloud revenue of $30.7 billion in the third quarter, slightly more than double the $15.2 billion it generated in the same period last year. But the revenue growth is only part of the story.

Google Cloud's operating income more than tripled to $11.1 billion, while its operating margin expanded from 23.7% to 36.2%. That's a remarkable improvement for a business that has historically operated with much thinner margins than Google's advertising operations.

Google is benefiting from its ability to offer customers a range of products from AI infrastructure to its Gemini models. It also designs its own Tensor Processing Units (TPUs), specialized chips built to handle demanding AI workloads.

These chips are becoming an increasingly important part of Google's business. Alphabet said TPU system sales made a meaningful contribution to third-quarter revenue growth, giving the company another way to profit from the enormous investments businesses are making in AI.

But there's an even more interesting number buried in Alphabet's earnings report.

Google Cloud ended the third quarter with a whopping $561 billion in backlog, representing contracted revenue that hasn't yet been recognized. That's a massive amount of business already under contract, and management expects to recognize just over 55% of that backlog as revenue over the next 24 months.

For investors, the backlog provides some visibility into Google Cloud's future revenue. It also suggests that the company's recent growth isn't simply the result of customers experimenting with AI. Businesses are making substantial financial commitments to Google's infrastructure.

And Google has another advantage. Unlike many AI infrastructure providers, Alphabet can support its enormous investments with an established, highly profitable advertising business.

Google Services generated $96.3 billion in third-quarter revenue, an 11% increase from a year earlier. Search and other advertising revenue grew 12%, providing additional evidence that AI hasn't undermined Google's core business.

In fact, Pichai said AI is contributing to increased search activity, with year-over-year query growth reaching its highest rate in five years.

That's an encouraging combination: Google's traditional business continues to grow while Cloud becomes an increasingly important source of revenue and profits.

Building enough computing capacity to satisfy customers isn't cheap. Alphabet's capital expenditure bill was $51.4 billion in the third quarter, and the company reported negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion.

GOOGL Free Cash Flow (Quarterly) data by YCharts

Alphabet is also relying on third-party computing capacity to help meet demand. CFO Anat Ashkenazi warned that this arrangement could pressure Google Cloud's operating margins in the near term. That's something investors shouldn't overlook. Google Cloud's revenue growth is outstanding, but the company must continue investing heavily to deliver on its commitments.

The backlog is encouraging, but it doesn't guarantee that every dollar of future revenue will translate into profits.

The company is spending heavily on AI, but it's necessary spending. Alphabet's future largely depends on its ability to incorporate AI into its offerings and to offer world-class cloud computing services.

Google Cloud is growing rapidly, generating substantial operating profits, and accumulating an enormous backlog of contracted business. Meanwhile, Google's advertising operations continue to provide the financial muscle needed to support its AI investments.

Pichai's announcement gives shareholders something tangible to celebrate. Google's investments are paying off in a tangible way -- and Google Cloud's backlog suggests there's plenty more business waiting to be delivered.
